content: Omeprazole is generally well tolerated, but it can cause a range of side effects, some of which are more common than others. Below is a detailed breakdown of the adverse effects associated with its use, based on clinical trial data and post-marketing reports. Side Effects Occurring in 1% or More of Patients U.S. Clinical Trials In a U.S. clinical trial involving 465 patients with conditions such as duodenal ulcers, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and resistant ulcers, the following side effects were reported in at least 1% of patients taking omeprazole: Headache Diarrhea Abdominal pain Nausea Upper respiratory infections (URI) Dizziness Vomiting Rash Constipation Cough Asthenia (weakness) Back pain International Clinical Trials In international clinical trials involving 2,631 patients, the following side effects were reported in at least 1% of patients treated with omeprazole: Abdominal pain Asthenia (weakness) Constipation Diarrhea Flatulence Nausea Vomiting Acid regurgitation Headache Side Effects Occurring in Less Than 1% of Patients Additional side effects, reported in less than 1% of patients during clinical trials or post-marketing surveillance, are categorized by organ system: pylori Eradication When omeprazole is used in combination with other drugs for the eradication of Helicobacter pylori, no new or unique side effects have been observed. Adverse effects are consistent with those already known for omeprazole, clarithromycin, or amoxicillin. Triple Therapy (Omeprazole/Clarithromycin/Amoxicillin) In clinical trials involving 274 patients, the most common side effects were: Diarrhea (14%) Taste disturbances (10%) Headache (7%) These side effects occurred at rates similar to those seen with the individual antimicrobial agents. Dual Therapy (Omeprazole/Clarithromycin) In clinical trials involving 346 patients, the following side effects were observed, which were not commonly reported with omeprazole alone: Taste disturbances (15%) Tongue discoloration (2%) Rhinitis (2%) Pharyngitis (1%) Flu-like symptoms (1%)
